Speedwell memos.com. All of our memos are there. For this week's Memo,

disclaimer, it is highly likely I will be mispronouncing some of these Swedish names, so apologies for that.
And without further ado, let us begin. First section. Founding History
Swedish-born Jens Van Bar worked a bag of jobs before finding his calling. He worked in leisure
travel in Vietnam, started a secondhand sportswear store, and ran an advertising agency. He'd eventually
get an MBA in Australia. And thereafter, became the head of makeup for Oriflame Sri Lanka operations.
All along the way, he kept in touch with his childhood friend, Frederick Osterberg,
who was working at the sports website, Sportel. They watched many of their
peers get rich during the dot-com boom and started thinking about things they
could do together. The idea of sports betting was floated, but there were a plethora of sites that were
already working on that and poker. However, they wondered if there wasn't something more in the gambling
realm they could offer. While they themselves were never big gamblers, they thought online gambling
had a lot of potential. The idea of live streaming roulette from Monte Carlo to someone across the
world sitting at home became a powerful vision for them.
They decided to build an online live casino business that would allow players to feel like
they were playing in a real casino from the comfort of their home.
The problems, though, were numerous, from getting the picture quality and streaming experience
high enough, to figuring out the legality of what they were doing.
One of the first people to get the idea pitched to them was Unibet founder, Onstra Strom.
Prenticeses Unibet was an early gaming operator with sports betting in digital slots.
But the idea was too early.
The picture quality and bandwidth lag made for an unimpressive experience.
He would pass, but thought there was long-term potential.
While the pair couldn't get a key customer interested yet, they did find some investors, with the help
from Richard Hedita.
Richard was previously the head of tech and media investments for London and regional
properties limited, which was essentially a family office for the British real estate
billionaires, Richard and Ian Livingstone.
Securing that investment was critical.
to building a real product.
Richard Hedita became the third co-founder and involved in the operations as creative director.
In 2006, with the seed investment from Richard Livingstone, Evolution Gaming was born.
Next section. Business History.
Their first move was to use their funds to build the first live casino studio in Riga,
a location close enough to Europe was sufficient, affordable, multilingual labor.
In 2007, it was completed, and the first customer started broadcasting live.
The product still required a hard sell from the founders.
Few gaming operators were interested, as they were unsure players would like the product,
especially since they were convinced it would regularly crash.
In 2009, though, Unibet trialed the product.
While initial expectations were low, within a year they had worked out most of the
the kinks, and the product was working without any hiccups.
Just a year later, in 2010, the first gaming operator experimented with it by
dedicating an entire website's tab to live casino on the top of their site.
In short order, the question of whether this would be something customers wanted was settled forever.
The operator's website activity quickly increased 400% year over year.
It turned out, players not only found the live casino games entertaining, but also trusted
them more than their digital equivalent, which they felt were more likely to be tampered with.
Evolution's sales pitch became much easier as gaming operators saw a clear proof point and lined up
to be added as carriers of Evolution's games.
The online-only-only gaming operators often started with just sports betting or poker, but
were increasingly leveraging their captive user base by trying to cross-sell them at their gambling
products. These operators often did not develop their own games, but carried
games from a variety of suppliers. Live Casino was an entirely new product for them to upsell their
users on, and it would also differentiate them from other operators who lacked that category.
Once one operator saw how popular it was with players, all of them needed it.
Yenz and Frederick decided to move to Malta, the center of online gaming in Europe,
and worked on getting more licenses for other countries.
They wanted to be the first in every market, so they wouldn't give competitors who were starting to develop
similar offerings a chance to catch up.
In 2011, they would become the first operator in the newly regulated Italian market.
This volume pushed their Latvian studio to critical mass and operated 24-7 to meet player demand.
Being first to win licenses would be a mainstay of their growth strategy.
In 2012, they became the first certified live casino supplier in the Danish markets.
And in 2013, they partnered with the land-based casino to be the first to be certified to offer games in Spain.
Whereas since inception, the focus was only on serving desktop PCs, as early smartphones weren't
conducive to an enjoyable gaming experience. By 2012, the devices and connectivity
environment improved enough that evolution launched mobile gaming.
desktops were still vastly more popular for years to come.
Parentheses, by 2014, only 13% of revenue was generated on mobile devices.
But being there early would allow them to benefit when the preferred playing device flipped
flipped to mobile several years later.
All of the data they were gathering from their ever-growing player base
was also helping them improve security and anti-fraud systems,
as well as help increase dealer consistency.
Mistakes, like spinning a roulette wheel too slowly, can inadvertently give players an edge.
This further attached operators to evolution.
Noticing that the tables they offered operators were leading to a similar player experience,
they started thinking of how to offer unique and custom experience to help operators
differentiate themselves.
Evolution would offer custom and dedicated tables to operators, including dealers who spoke
different languages, which was important for them to not only differentiate,
but build customer trust.
The dedicated tables were also helpful in winning over land-based casino operators.
These land-based casinos wanted to increase player loyalty and stay top of mind,
since many customers only visited a handful of times a year, if that.
An app, with tables branded in the casino's name, would help the operator achieve both goals.
Additionally, it gave land-based casinos a position in the quickly growing online gaming world,
which alleviated some concerns that the online gaming would pressure land-based casino gambling.
Now, though, the live casino experience was good enough that they started moving
their focus on to new games. They launched one of their first game iterations,
three-card poker, and bet behind for Blackjack in 2014. At the time, they noted that customers are now
now making a larger initial investment and therefore often go dedicated with the live environment from the start.
Not only are dedicated tables more profitable for evolution gaming, but the higher
upfront investment made operators more willing to promote live casino to get a return, and
less likely to engage with the many competitor products that were starting
to spring up. By the end of 2014, Evolution had 120 tables and was the clear, dominant live casino
provider of Europe. Revenues were just shy 50 million euros, with EBTA margins at 35%. With
With the sizable business that was growing rapidly, Evolution decided to go public.
They felt the transparency of being a public company could help them when dealing
with state gaming institutions and regulators. In March 2015, evolution
gaming started trading on the NASDAQ First North Premier Exchange, which is a smaller European
NASDAQ exchange for growth companies. At the time, they were valued at just $340 million.
Prenticeseses a few years later, it would be trading on the main NASDAQ, Stockholm Exchange.
The company didn't need to raise money in the IPO, but many shareholders partially
partially cashed out, with existing holders selling almost 40% of the company in the offering.
Jens Van Bar and Frederick Ostenberg each took their ownership down from around 17% to 10%
and seed investor, Richard Livingstone, sold his 33% stake, down to 16 and a half.
Post-IPO, evolution would continue to sign-up operators with a focus on expanding
their studios to accommodate more dedicated tables.
Yens Van Barre noted in 2015 that they were launching more games beyond the typical five-core games
they provided.
There also was an inflection in mobile gaming popularity in 2015, and total revenues from mobile
reached 27%. As Jens Van Bar felt that Evolution was in a strong position,
he would step down as CEO, but stay on as chairman of the board. Martin Carlson, an external hire,
was appointed as Evolution Gaming's new CEO. Around this time, they made another key hire,
Todd Ha Schalter, as their chief product officer. How important he would become to
evolution was unknown until a few years later when he helped create a whole
new category of live casino games called live game shows, the first of which Dreamcatchers was
launched in 2017. This new category of games was novel, entertaining, and perhaps most critically,
appealed to the more casual gambler who didn't want to play table games.
Many gamblers first come to an operator's site for sports betting and see the live casino
tab on the website or in the app, but all too often are too intimidated or
disinterested to play table games like Blackjack. But the game show category provides very entertaining games
that are also simple to play. Todd Halshalter talks about how this category changes the dynamics of operators
cross-cell in the press release below. This is an excerpt from the 2017 press release
This is a monumentous launch for us because Dreamcatchers will expose live casino
to players who don't play table games and therefore don't play live casino.
There are millions of slots, bingo, and other players who we are reaching out with this product.
It is intentionally simple and friendly to play along.
And with the potential for the 2x and 7x multipliers to keep hitting sequentially,
players can win thousands of times their initial bet, just like in slots.
It is almost like a game show that you can play along with at home.
Both slots and table game players will find it as familiar in an enjoyable way to play.
We really tried hard to make Dreamcatchers a game that will expand the live casino space,
and we hope the players will find it as fun as we do.
Operators are constantly telling us that they want to cross-sell live into other player
verticals. So we started thinking a ways to do that.
But when it came to slot, bingo, pull tab players, the problem was not making them
aware of live, but simply that they don't want to play table games.
So we started brainstorming about games that have no cards, dice, or even a table.
The lucky wheel seemed intriguing, but the house advantage was too high, and it lacked the ability
to win large amounts.
By adding the 2x and 7x multipliers that will hit fairly frequently, we brought the house
advantage in line with other online slots. It made it incredibly exciting.
So now, we have a real tool for our partners to cross-sell to slots and other non-table game players.
Evolution's growth continued to be strong, as they benefited from the online gaming market exploding,
and revenues reaching 250 million euros in 2018 were up 500% in just five years.
